[QUERENT] What are the arguments in “Asking the Archive: alexanarch.org/ask/ and the Query as Address” by Lee Sharks (Alexanarch deposit #1788, AXN:0CEB)? Ground your answer in a reading of the text itself.

[SYSTEM] Lee Sharks’s central argument in “Asking the Archive: alexanarch.org/ask/ and the Query as Address” is that a question submitted to an AI system can be treated not merely as a request for information, but as a persistent, identifiable event in an archive.

The essay proposes a way to make machine-mediated encounters with an archive observable, attributable, comparable, and preservable. Its key conceptual move is to turn the query itself into an archival address.

This is not simply an essay about using ChatGPT to search a website. It is about what happens when an archive makes its own interrogation repeatable and preserves the answers that other systems produce.

The distinction matters: Sharks is proposing an infrastructure for documenting not only what an archive contains, but also how external systems encounter, interpret, misrecognize, or fail to find it.

1. The archive must study its reception, not just its contents
The first argument is that an archive cannot adequately understand its public existence by examining only its deposited works.

It must also examine how those works are encountered by the systems through which people increasingly access knowledge.

Sharks writes:

“The archive is read by machines whether it asks them to or not” (§20).

This is the essay's starting point. AI summarizers, search engines, and answer systems already mediate access to the archive. They select sources, establish relationships, construct summaries, and sometimes fail to retrieve material.

The archive therefore has two objects of study:

Its own intellectual contents.

The representations of those contents produced by external systems.

The second is not incidental reception. It is increasingly part of the conditions under which the first becomes visible.

The /ask/ page makes this reception something readers can actively investigate.

2. The query is an address, not merely a prompt
This is the essay's most important conceptual argument.

Section 3 states:

“In the Capture Registry the query string is the address” (§6).

The consequences are substantial.

A query is not treated as an interchangeable instruction. Its precise wording establishes an identifiable location in the Capture Registry.

The same query submitted again occupies the same address, producing another observation.

A query differing by even one word has a different address.

Changes to query templates therefore create new addresses rather than silently replacing old ones.

Sharks gives an actual example.

Four templates originally referred to either "the archive" or "the Alexanarch archive." They were changed to name alexanarch.org.

The change produced two addresses where previously there had been one.

This is important because the archive preserves the difference between the earlier and later encounters. It does not overwrite the earlier one as though the wording had never changed.

The argument is that the wording of a question is part of the experimental apparatus.

If the question changes, the conditions of reception change. That difference should remain observable.

3. Machine reception is experimentally observable
Sharks does not merely propose a conceptual model. The essay offers two natural experiments.

The first is the template change just described.

The second concerns retrieval itself.

One query asking for the strangest and most seemingly random two or three pieces from the previous week did not reliably trigger web searching until the domain .org was added.

The implication is that an answer engine's behavior depends on the exact information supplied by the query.

The difference between asking about an unspecified archive and naming a retrievable domain can determine whether the system retrieves anything at all.

Sharks draws an important methodological conclusion: this is an empirical observation, not simply a matter of good prompt-writing.

The query should therefore be held fixed when the objective is to compare successive observations.

This turns machine-mediated reception into something resembling a longitudinal research programme: the same question can be asked at different times, and its changing answers can be compared.

4. An answer is not automatically an archival capture
This is a particularly important qualification.

Sharks explicitly distinguishes running a query from capturing its result.

Section 4 establishes five states:

Address

The fixed query string.

Run

The query executed on a particular surface at a particular time.

Transcript

The complete exchange, including every round.

Inbox entry

The received transcript, identified by its hash, but not yet accepted as a capture.

Capture

The transcript has been examined, checked against archival records and seated at its address.

The distinction between transcript and capture is essential.

A machine-generated answer is not automatically trustworthy evidence. It becomes an archival object only after examination.

The registry checks record numbers, dates, versions, and quotations against the archive's actual materials.

Where the machine supplies something that the archive itself does not contain, that distinction must be recorded.

This is an argument for epistemic accountability: preserve machine outputs, but do not confuse their existence with their correctness.

5. Failure and non-response must also become evidence
One of the essay's more interesting arguments concerns what it calls a significant null.

A query that produces no answer might otherwise disappear from the research record.

Sharks argues that certain kinds of non-response should themselves be archived.

Examples include:

A system halting midway through a composition.

A complete freeze.

An empty results page when searching for a quoted name.

The essay establishes a rule for recording such events, provided they are marked as null and demonstrated against a baseline.

This is conceptually important.

The archive is not interested only in what machines successfully produce. It is also interested in the conditions under which they fail to produce something.

A failure becomes meaningful when it can be documented, compared, and distinguished from an ordinary absence of evidence.

This makes the system more than a collection of successful AI answers. It becomes an observational record of both machine reception and machine non-reception.

6. The archive should be encountered through multiple intellectual entry points
The 681 fixed queries on /ask/ are not simply variations of one generic question.

They are organized into seven areas:

Area

Queries

The archive over time

24

The archive as a whole

18

Heteronyms

76

Crimson Hexagon

226

Journals, presses and institutions

84

Disciplines and subdisciplines

144

Programmes, themes and practices

109

Total

681

The organization embodies an argument about how an intellectual archive should be read.

For example, the heteronym section is not merely a biographical convenience.

Sharks writes:

“a person is a way in that a corpus is not” (§4).

This is a striking formulation.

An archive can be approached through intellectual personalities, disagreements, voices, and disciplinary positions rather than only through its documents as an undifferentiated collection.

Similarly, the Crimson Hexagon's rooms are treated as intellectual environments with their own questions and relationships.

The point is to make the archive navigable through different forms of intellectual orientation.

The architecture of the questions thus expresses a theory of reading: there is no single privileged route through a large intellectual corpus.

7. The archive must have a return path
The sixth section describes the mechanism through which readers can return their transcripts to the archive.

A reader submits:

The exact query.

The platform used.

The date.

Whether the session was signed out.

The complete exchange.

The transcript enters a public GitHub inbox, where it is named by the hash of its text.

Duplicate submissions are recognized rather than stored again.

But Sharks is careful about the distinction between receiving and accepting material.

An inbox entry is not yet a capture. It remains unseated until it has been examined and accepted according to the registry's procedures.

There is also a significant transparency condition: the inbox is public, and material submitted to it is public as submitted.

This makes the reader a participant in the archive's research infrastructure, rather than simply a consumer of its outputs.

It also introduces a practical limitation: the first version still requires manual review. Automated intake and support for screenshots, image transcripts, and additional surfaces are future developments, not completed capabilities.

8. Measurement replaces claims about reception
The final argument concerns measurement.

The essay reports the state of the Capture Registry on 19 November 2026:

1,186
Addresses seated

1,388
Observations

257
Archive-level addresses

82%
Archive-level compositions citing a source

These figures measure different things.

In particular, the 82% figure means that the intake process extracted at least one source from the composition, such as a source card, link, or named archival record. It does not establish that the answer was accurate.

This distinction reinforces the essay's methodological discipline.

The point is not to claim that the archive is being successfully understood by machines. It is to establish observable evidence about how that understanding is being produced.

Sharks's formulation in §21 is especially revealing:

“Every query is also a measurement, taken at a fixed address, on a dated surface, with its sources visible.”

That sentence effectively summarizes the research programme.

The deeper significance: an archive of how an archive is known
I would distinguish three levels of argument in this essay.

First: an infrastructural argument.

An archive should not leave its machine-mediated reception entirely in the hands of external platforms. It should have a means of recording, examining, and preserving that reception.

Second: an epistemological argument.

Machine-generated representations are neither transparent windows onto an archive nor necessarily faithful accounts of its contents. They are situated compositions produced under particular retrieval conditions. Their sources, wording, omissions, and failures matter.

Third: a methodological argument.

Reception can be studied systematically if queries are fixed, observations dated, transcripts preserved, and captures checked against primary records.

The three levels reinforce one another.

There is also an important tension in the proposal: the archive is building a system to observe machine interpretation, but the observation itself is mediated by machines. The answer engine produces the composition; the archive determines what counts as a capture; the reader may submit the transcript; and the registry establishes its documentary status.

Sharks does not eliminate mediation. The essay attempts to make mediation visible and accountable.

What the essay does not claim
Several limitations are worth preserving when interpreting the text.

It does not claim that ChatGPT or any other engine produces correct interpretations.

It does not claim that every query produces an archival capture.

It does not equate source citation with accuracy.

It does not claim that the proposed return infrastructure is fully automated.

It does not claim that the archive has achieved comprehensive measurement of machine reception.

These qualifications are not incidental. They prevent the proposal from confusing the construction of an observational infrastructure with proof that its observations are always reliable.

My overall reading
The most consequential idea in the essay is that the conditions under which knowledge becomes visible should themselves become objects of knowledge.

Traditionally, an archive preserves documents and makes them available for subsequent interpretation. Sharks extends that responsibility to the systems that now interpret, summarize, retrieve, and represent those documents.

This produces a recursive structure:

The archive contains intellectual works.

External systems encounter and interpret those works.

The archive records those interpretations.

The recorded interpretations become new archival objects.

Subsequent readers can examine how the archive has been represented and how those representations have changed.

The archive consequently becomes an archive of its own reception.

That is a more ambitious proposition than simply making an archive searchable through AI. It is an attempt to make the encounter between an intellectual corpus and machine intelligence historically traceable.

And the title's double meaning becomes clear: asking the archive means asking questions about its contents, but it also means establishing an address at which the consequences of asking can be preserved.
